paragraphs: Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum element in the unsorted part of an array and exchanges it with the first element of that part.

blocks.text: Algorithm

items.text: Read N and the N array elements.
For each position i from 0 to N − 2, set min_index = i.
Scan positions j = i + 1 through N − 1. If a[j] < a[min_index], update min_index = j.
Exchange a[i] and a[min_index] if they are different positions. The prefix through i is now sorted.
After all passes, display the array.

blocks.text: The smallest remaining element is selected on every pass, so the sorted prefix grows by one. The algorithm makes N(N−1)/2 comparisons: Θ(N²) time in best and worst cases and O(1) extra space. The ordinary swap-based version is not stable.

paragraphs: Predefined functions are supplied by a library; user-defined functions are written by the programmer for a specific task.

rows: Declarations are obtained through the appropriate header.
Declare a prototype before use and provide a matching definition.

paragraphs: A local variable is declared within a block; a global variable is declared outside functions at file scope.

rows: Its name is visible from its declaration to the end of its block.
Its name is visible from its declaration to the end of the translation unit, subject to shadowing.
Ordinary non-static locals usually have automatic storage duration.
File-scope objects have static storage duration.
An uninitialized automatic int has an indeterminate value.
An uninitialized static-duration int is zero-initialized.

blocks.text: Scope and lifetime are different: a block-local static variable still has block scope but retains its value throughout program execution. Global visibility is governed by declarations, not automatic access from every possible function or file.

paragraphs: Recursion repeats through function calls; iteration repeats through a loop.

rows: A function calls itself directly or indirectly.
A while, do–while or for loop repeats its body.
A reachable base case and progressing recursive arguments.
A condition and updates that eventually end the loop.
Separate active calls retain their local state; typically uses O(depth) call storage.
State is maintained in loop variables; simple numerical loops usually need constant extra storage.
Call overhead; natural for recursive definitions or structures.
Avoids repeated function calls; natural for straightforward repetition.

paragraphs: In linear search, compare the required element with array values from the start to the end.

blocks.text: Algorithm

items.text: Read n, the n elements, and key ele.
For i=0 through n−1, compare a[i] with ele.
On the first match, report position i+1 and stop.
If no match occurs, report not found.

blocks.text: For [20,12,1,4,9], key 4 is found at position 4. Sorting is unnecessary. Worst-case time is O(n); a first-element match takes constant time.

paragraphs: Binary search takes O(log n) comparisons in the worst case because each unsuccessful comparison discards about half the remaining candidates.

blocks.text: After k halvings, about n/2^k candidates remain. Reaching one candidate requires k of order log₂n. A middle-element match is the best case, O(1). The array must be sorted consistently with the comparisons, and indexed access is assumed.

paragraphs: The ordinary selection-sort method takes Θ(n²) comparisons in the best, average and worst cases.

blocks.text: It scans n−1 candidates, then n−2, down to 1. The total is n(n−1)/2 comparisons, even for an already sorted array. There are at most n−1 exchanges, and extra space is O(1). For n=5, the scans make 4+3+2+1=10 comparisons.

blocks.text: Algorithm for ascending data

items.text: Set first=0 and last=n−1.
While first<=last, recompute mid=first+(last−first)/2.
If a[mid]==ele, report mid+1 and stop.
If a[mid]>ele, set last=mid−1; otherwise set first=mid+1.
If first>last, report not found.

blocks.text: Example sorted array: [1,4,9,12,20]. The key 12 is at position 4. The interval halves at each failed comparison, giving O(log n) worst-case time.

paragraphs: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by inserting the next key into its proper place.

items.text: For i from 1 to n−1, save key=a[i] and set j=i−1.
Shift larger prefix elements one position right while j>=0 and a[j]>key.
Store key at a[j+1]. Repeat for every remaining element.

blocks.text: Each displayed prefix is sorted. Strict > shifts preserve equal-element order. Best-case time is O(n), worst-case O(n²), with O(1) extra space.
